angle: The bottleneck in agent systems is orchestration and I/O, not GPUs; design for concurrency and batching.
sourceTitle: Kog is going deeper to squeeze more inference out of GPUs
linkedinPost:
“GPUs are bad for agents” is mostly a coordination problem disguised as hardware criticism.

TechCrunch covered Kog’s claim that GPUs can handle agentic workflows if you architect right. From the FDE trenches, I agree: the real enemy is tiny, chatty steps with network I/O between them. Your GPU sits idle while your agent waits on tools.

What’s worked in production:
- Batch across steps: accumulate small tool calls and decode bursts together; don’t launch kernels for 8 tokens.
- Keep state on-device: reuse KV caches across tool-use turns where possible to avoid re‑encoding the world.
- Overlap I/O and compute: async function calls while the model plans the next move; stop serializing everything.
- Use a “planner” small model and a “doer” bigger model on the same card; pin routes by cost/latency.

In one customer flow, 70% of wall time was network waits, not tokens. We cut median latency 40% by reducing cross‑service hops and adopting adaptive batching—no hardware change.

The Kog piece is a good nudge: fix orchestration before shopping for more GPUs. Where’s your agent spending its wall time? #AIEngineering #LLM #FDE
xPost: Agents don’t stall because “GPUs are bad.” They stall on orchestration and I/O. Batch tiny steps, reuse KV, overlap tool calls with decode, and route planner/doer models smartly. Optimize wall time before buying GPUs. #AIEngineering #FDE
